author: clara-bennett
title: Missing Your Mom: When You Reach for the Phone to Call Her
dek: Missing your mom can arrive in a parking lot, with your hand already on the phone. A three-minute note for what you were going to tell her.
seo_title: Missing Your Mom: When You Reach for the Phone to Call Her
seo_description: Missing your mom when you reach for the phone to call her: a short note for what you would have told her, step by step, for the moment it happens.
pull_quote: Reaching for the phone is not a mistake. It is what love does out of habit.
body_html:
It happens on a Tuesday, in a grocery store parking lot. Something small goes right, or something small goes wrong, and your hand is already moving toward the phone. Your thumb knows where her name is.

You know what you were going to say. You can almost hear how she would answer: the way she said your name when she picked up, the short pause before she asked how you were really doing.

Then you remember.

Missing your mom does not always look like crying at a graveside. Often it looks like this: a woman standing next to her car with a phone in her hand and nobody to call with it.

Why missing your mom shows up in ordinary moments

People expect the hard days. Her birthday. Mother's Day. The date itself. On those days someone may check on you. Nobody checks on you on a Tuesday in a parking lot.

But the ordinary days are where she lived. The recipe you cannot quite remember. A sweater on a stranger that looks like one she wore. News you want to tell someone, and the only someone you want is her.

The phone is its own kind of ambush, because calling her was something your hands did before you thought about it. For years, maybe decades, she was the person you called. Your hand still knows that.

Reaching for the phone is not a mistake. It is what love does out of habit.

Reaching for the phone is not a mistake. It is what love does out of habit.

Her number may still be in your phone. Some daughters keep it. Some keep her last voicemail and cannot play it. None of this needs explaining to anyone.

The thing you were going to tell her

What stays in your hand, after you remember, is the thing you were going to say. It is usually small. What the mechanic said. That the tomatoes finally came in. That your daughter lost her first tooth. Small things are what those calls were made of.

The words have nowhere to go, and that is a large part of what hurts. So here is one place to put them: a short note called what I would have told you.

It is not a letter. It has no greeting and no goodbye. You do not have to say how you feel, or sum anything up. You write only the thing itself, the way you would have said it on the phone. It takes about three minutes, and all you need is the notes app on your phone or the back of a receipt.

It is a small thing to do in a hard moment. If it feels like too much today, leave it. The note can wait, and it can also go unwritten.

The "what I would have told you" note, step by step

  1. Stay where you are. Sit down if you can: the car seat, a bench, the edge of the bed. Rest the phone in your lap and take one slow breath before you do anything else.
  2. Open a blank note. Use the notes app or a scrap of paper. At the top, put the day of the week and the words What I would have told you.
  3. Write the thing itself. One to three sentences, in the words you would have used on the phone. "The car is making that noise again." "I got the job." You do not need to add that she is gone. The note already knows.
  4. Add her answer, only if you can hear it. One line, in her words. If you cannot hear it today, leave that line empty. An empty line is honest.
  5. Stop. Read the note once and close it. Three minutes is enough. It does not need to be longer, or better written, or finished.

As an example only: a daughter might write, Tuesday. What I would have told you: the hydrangea you gave me came up blue this year, not pink. I do not know why. Under it, her mother's line: It's the soil, honey. That is the whole note.

What to do with the note afterwards

You have a few choices.

  • Keep them in one place. One running note in your phone with her name as the title, newest on top. Or one envelope in a drawer for the paper ones. You do not have to reread them. They only need a place.
  • Say one out loud. In the car, with the windows up, read the note once in your normal phone voice. Some daughters find the sound of it harder than the writing. Some find it closer.
  • Let it go. You can delete the note or throw the receipt away. It was written to give the words a place for a minute. Keeping it is optional.

One caution. If her number is no longer hers, a text sent to it may reach a stranger, and a stranger's reply is a hard thing to receive. Keep the note in your own notes, addressed to no number at all.

What you might notice

You might notice nothing. The note may feel as flat as a shopping list, and you may wonder why you bothered. That happens, and it does not mean you did it wrong or that you miss her less.

It may hurt more for a moment. Seeing the words written down, with no answer coming, can make the quiet on her end louder. If that happens, put the phone down and look at what is in front of you: the steering wheel, the trees at the edge of the lot, your own hands. Give it a minute before you drive.

You might feel her close for a second. You might feel foolish. I cannot tell you this note will help. It is only somewhere for the words to go.

If the weight is there all the time, or if you are thinking of harming yourself, a doctor, a counselor or a crisis line is the right place to turn.

When to use it

  • In the moment itself, when your hand is already on the phone and you have three minutes before you have to be anywhere.
  • Later that night, if the moment came in a meeting or a checkout line and you had to keep your face still and carry on.
  • On days with news, good or bad, the kind she would have heard before anyone else.

This is not a daily assignment, and there is nothing to keep up. Some weeks there may be five notes. Some months there may be none. The note is for the moment when it comes, not for a schedule.

Questions women ask about missing your mom

Why does missing my mom show up on ordinary days? The ordinary days are where she lived. A recipe you cannot quite remember, a sweater on a stranger, news you want to tell someone. Nobody checks on you on a Tuesday in a parking lot.

Why do I still reach for the phone to call my mom? Calling her was something your hands did before you thought about it, for years, maybe decades. Your hand still knows that. Reaching for the phone is not a mistake.

What can I do with the things I want to tell my mom? One place to put them is a short note called what I would have told you, written the way you would have said it on the phone. It takes about three minutes. I cannot tell you it will help, and the note can also go unwritten.

The phone is one place she lived in your day. Her things are another. If you have a recipe card or a list in her handwriting, there is a small ritual for it in these ways to remember your mom through her recipes and handwriting.

You do not have to stop reaching for the phone. You do not have to train yourself out of it. There is nothing here to fix.

author: clara-bennett
title: Ways to Remember Your Mom: Recipes, Handwriting and Small Rituals
dek: Ways to remember your mom with what was hers: a recipe card, an object, a phrase, and one small handwriting ritual for a quiet evening.
seo_title: Ways to Remember Your Mom: Recipes and Handwriting
seo_description: Ways to remember your mom at home: her recipes, her handwriting, a phrase she used, and a step-by-step ritual of copying one recipe card by hand.
pull_quote: The card holds what she wrote down, and the rest was only in her hands.
body_html:
There is a drawer somewhere with her handwriting in it. A grocery list. A birthday card. A recipe card with a stain in the corner, from the year she made that dish for everyone.

You may not open the drawer often. Some days you cannot. Some days you open it only to see how she made her capital letters.

When you look for ways to remember your mom, you are often shown large things: a memorial, a framed portrait, a day set aside. This entry is about the small ones, the kind that fit on a kitchen table on an ordinary evening.

Small ways to remember your mom with what was hers

So much of a mother lives in small, repeated things. Three of them tend to stay in a house long after she is gone: a recipe, an object and a phrase.

A recipe. The card, the pan she always used, the note in the margin that says less salt or double this in ink that has started to fade. Cooking from it can feel like standing next to her. It can also feel unbearable. You might make the dish once and cry the whole time. You might not be ready to make it at all.

An object. Her reading glasses. A wooden spoon. The mug nobody else was allowed to use. Some daughters put the object back to work and stir the soup with her spoon. Others keep it where it can be touched without being looked at, in a coat pocket or the back of a drawer.

A phrase. What she said when you left the house. What she said when something broke. Some daughters say it out loud in the spot where she would have said it: at the door, at the stove, at the end of a call. A daughter might hear it come out of her own mouth one evening and stand still in the middle of the kitchen.

You do not need all three, and you do not need a ritual that looks a certain way. You only need something that feels like her.

Why her handwriting stops you

Handwriting is hers the way her voice was. The slant. The way she crossed her sevens. The abbreviations nobody else used.

A recipe card is also a record of use. The stain. The soft corner. The line she crossed out and wrote again. And it is never the whole recipe. The card holds what she wrote down, and the rest was only in her hands.

The card holds what she wrote down, and the rest was only in her hands.

That is why the ritual below is built around the card and not around the cooking. You do not have to turn on the stove. You do not have to write anything to her. You only have to follow her hand with yours.

The recipe card ritual, step by step

Set aside one quiet evening and about fifteen minutes. You will need one card in her handwriting, a blank index card or a sheet of paper, a pen and a clear table. If you have no recipe card, anything she wrote will do: a list, an envelope, the inside of a birthday card.

If it feels like too much once her card is in front of you, stop there and put it back. It will keep.

  1. Clear a space. Wipe the table and dry your hands. Lay her card down flat, away from the sink and the stove.
  2. Look before you read. Take in the card as a thing she held: the stain, the crease, the color of the ink, the places where she pressed harder.
  3. Read it out loud once. Go slowly, exactly as she wrote it, with her abbreviations and her notes in the margin.
  4. Copy it by hand. Write it onto the blank card line by line. Keep her wording, her spelling and her order. Do not correct anything, even the parts that make no sense.
  5. Add one thing the card does not say. In a corner of your copy, write one detail only her hands knew, if you remember one. She used the blue bowl. She never measured the flour. If you do not remember, write I do not know and leave it there.
  6. Put hers away safely. Take a photo of her card, then slide the original into an envelope, somewhere flat and dry. Your copy is the one that can live in the kitchen and collect its own stains.

You can cook from your copy next week, next year or never. As an example only: a daughter might copy her mother's pie crust card and leave the copy on the counter for a month before she buys flour. Another might never bake it, and keep the copy on the refrigerator.

What you might notice

You might notice nothing. Copying the card may feel like copying any list, and you may finish wondering what it was for.

It may hurt more for a moment, most often at the third step. Her words in your voice can land harder than her words on paper. If that happens, stop reading and sit with your hand flat on the table until the room feels steady again. You can go on, or you can finish another day.

You might see that your handwriting looks like hers in places, or nothing like hers at all. You might find a gap in the card: an ingredient with no amount, an oven with no temperature, a step she never wrote because she never needed to. You do not have to fill the gap. It was part of how she cooked.

I cannot promise the copy will comfort you. It is one way of keeping something of hers in use instead of in a drawer.

If the heaviness never lifts at all, or if you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please turn to a doctor, a counselor or a crisis line.

When to use it

  • On a quiet evening when nothing has to be cooked and nobody needs you for a quarter of an hour.
  • Before a day the dish belonged to, a holiday or her birthday, if you want your copy ready and her card kept clear of the stove.
  • When something new turns up in her handwriting, in a box, a coat pocket or the back of a cupboard.
  • With someone else at the table, a sister, a brother or your own child, each of you copying a different card, if you would rather not do this alone.

Once may be all you want. One card may be all there is. Nothing here has to be repeated or kept up.

Questions women ask about ways to remember your mom

What are small ways to remember your mom at home? Three things tend to stay in a house long after she is gone: a recipe, an object and a phrase. Some daughters stir the soup with her spoon, or say what she said at the door. You do not need all three.

What can I do with my mom's handwritten recipes? One thing is to copy a card by hand, line by line, in her wording and her spelling. Her card can go into an envelope, somewhere flat and dry, and your copy can live in the kitchen. You can cook from it next week, next year or never.

What if it hurts too much to look at my mom's handwriting? Some days you cannot open the drawer. If her card feels like too much once it is in front of you, put it back. It will keep.

The drawer is something you choose to open. Other moments choose you. For those, there is a short note you can write in the moment you reach for the phone to call her, for the thing you were going to say.

None of this is about moving on. Her card, her spoon, the thing she always said: they are still hers, and they are still in your house.
